v.why: One might expect a 3x3 conv to add a lot at the output edge whatever it replaces, but swapping in a near-equivalent 1x1 conv leaves little headroom compared with replacing none, pool or skip.
The obvious view is that a second conv path to the output is complementary, but parents that already have a 3x3 conv feeding the output are near their ceiling, so the gain shrinks.
Extra conv depth looks additive, but once edge 5 already carries a 3x3 conv into the output, a second copy gives a smaller marginal gain (saturation).
One might think parallel convs into node 2 reinforce each other, but node 2 already gets strong conv features through edge 2, so adding another saturates.
Upgrading the first edge looks important, but replacing a 1x1 conv with a 3x3 conv is a small step compared with replacing none, pool or skip.
A deeper path might seem to matter most when a strong shortcut already exists, but node 2 already has a strong conv input, so the headroom is reduced.
One might expect pooling to be harmless when upstream features are rich, but harmful edits cost more in strong parents and look harmless in weak ones because of floor effects.
Pooling on the output edge looks uniformly bad, but when it replaces none it adds a path instead of displacing a conv, so the effect is much less negative or even positive.
Edge 4 may seem redundant, but deleting a 3x3 conv removes real capacity, whereas deleting pool or skip costs little.
Skip on edge 3 might look like a minor change, but replacing none restores the residual input-to-output path, a large gain compared with swapping out a conv.
Pooling inside the cell may seem diluted when a conv follows, but parents with a conv on edge 5 are strong, so degrading the path that conv uses shows a larger drop.
Swapping between conv types sounds neutral, but downgrading from the best op loses accuracy, whereas the average replacement (none, pool, skip) gains.
A 1x1 conv might seem marginal, but replacing a parameter-free pool on the output edge adds learnable capacity where it matters most.
Replacing pool with conv can look like a lateral move, but pool on a path to the output is among the weakest choices, so upgrading it gives an above-average gain.
Edge 2 may look like a redundant intermediate link, but removing a 3x3 conv there costs depth, while removing a weak op costs nothing.
One might expect the first conv to work well together with downstream convs, but parents with a strong output conv already have high accuracy, so the gain is compressed by headroom.
Pooling on a side path seems harmless when another strong path exists, but harmful edits show up more in strong parents than in weak, floor-limited ones.
Conv on the direct input-to-output edge competes with skip and is not uniformly good, but replacing none adds a whole path, so the gain is much larger.
A conv into the output seems valuable in any context, but when edge 0 is none, node 1 outputs zeros and a conv on edge 4 has nothing to process.
One might expect edge 2 to matter more when edge 0 is weak, but with edge 0 set to none node 1 carries no signal, so a conv on edge 2 has nothing to transform.
